checks_performed: Read only the authorized source JSON and draft JSON; independently compared the exact universal target with the draft's final coverage.
Re-derived the perfect-matching characterization of 2-factors, including both directions and polynomial auxiliary-graph size.
Checked the q-edge and connected q−1-edge splice constructions, including q=1, witness-cycle validity, and edit accounting.
Checked all nil branches, small-n handling, girth and radius inequalities, separator obstruction, and low-degree isolation.
Checked the quantifiers and contraposition in the conditional sublinear-component routine.
Re-derived the complete-bipartite edit-distance lower bound and the Hamiltonian graph containing an n/3-component triangle factor.

Ran an integer/Fraction-only checker over all 33,867 labeled simple graphs through six vertices, all 75 graphs through four vertices for the matching gadget, 652,136 separator tests, 202,013 isolation tests, and explicit bipartite and triangle-factor families.

claims.claim: Existence of a 2-factor, and an explicit 2-factor when one exists, can be determined in polynomial time.
claims.evidence: At a vertex v, every perfect matching must match its d(v)−2 private dummies to distinct incidence vertices, leaving exactly two incidences, which can only be matched across original-edge links. The selected original edges therefore have degree two at every vertex. Conversely, a 2-factor matches its two used incidences across original edges and bijectively matches all remaining incidences to the d(v)−2 dummies. The gadget has polynomially many vertices and O(sum_v d(v)^2) edges, and general-graph perfect matching is polynomial-time. The exact checker confirmed the equivalence and extracted factors for every graph through four vertices.
claims.search_method: Direct proof of the matching-gadget bijection, polynomial-size analysis, and exhaustive exact small-graph validation.

claims.claim: If the 2-factor routine reports that none exists, returning (G,nil) is correct.
claims.evidence: Every Hamiltonian cycle is a spanning 2-regular subgraph. Hence a graph without a 2-factor cannot be Hamiltonian, and returning the unchanged graph with nil uses zero edits and is correct. The exhaustive checker confirmed this implication through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Necessary-condition proof plus exhaustive exact enumeration of all labeled graphs through six vertices.

claims.claim: If G has a 2-factor with q cycle components, one can add at most q edges and explicitly obtain a Hamiltonian cycle; if G is connected, at most q−1 additions suffice.
claims.evidence: Breaking one witness edge in each factor cycle produces q disjoint spanning paths; cyclically joining their endpoints requires at most q missing connector edges and yields one spanning cycle. For q=1 the original factor cycle needs no addition. If G is connected, after some factor cycles have been merged into a cycle D, an original edge xy crosses from D to an unmerged factor cycle C. Removing witness edges xx′ and yy′ and using xy plus x′y′ merges the two cycles; only x′y′ may be absent from G. Induction performs q−1 merges and retains an explicit cycle. Exhaustive checking through six vertices confirmed both bounds for every graph and every contained 2-factor.
claims.search_method: Constructive path joining and inductive two-edge splice proof, supplemented by exhaustive exact enumeration.

claims.claim: For every fixed real 0<c≤3, Sidestep(Hamiltonian Cycle,dist_e,n/c) is in FP.
claims.evidence: Small n is handled directly. A disconnected graph is non-Hamiltonian, and absence of a 2-factor is also a valid nil certificate. Otherwise the graph is connected and a computed 2-factor has q≤n/3 components because every simple factor cycle has at least three vertices. The connected splice adds at most q−1≤n/3≤n/c edges and supplies an explicit Hamiltonian cycle. Every operation is polynomial-time and preserves the labeled vertex set. The checker verified the strongest boundary c=3 for every graph through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Complete branch analysis and exact radius inequalities, with exhaustive boundary testing at c=3.

claims.claim: For arbitrary fixed c>0, the target is polynomially solvable on graphs whose girth is at least c.
claims.evidence: Disconnected graphs and graphs without a 2-factor admit the stated nil outputs. Otherwise the girth g is finite, each component of a computed 2-factor has at least g vertices, and qg≤n. Since g≥c, the splice uses at most q−1≤q≤n/g≤n/c additions. Forests cause no exception because they have no 2-factor. Connectivity, 2-factor computation, and splicing are polynomial-time. The exact checker verified qg≤n and the corresponding edit bound for every applicable graph through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Girth-versus-factor-component counting proof and exhaustive exact small-graph validation.

claims.claim: A general cheap non-Hamiltonicity edit is obtained from a component-count obstruction.
claims.evidence: Given the stated S and partition, deleting all inter-part edges makes H−S have at least p components. If a Hamiltonian cycle existed, deleting a nonempty S from that cycle would leave at most |S| path components, and adding other H−S edges could only merge them; for S empty, a Hamiltonian graph must be connected. Thus p>max{1,|S|} proves non-Hamiltonicity, and the assumed deletion count gives the radius. This verifies the conditional obstruction actually stated; it does not assert that such a cheap partition always exists or is always discoverable. Exhaustive checks confirmed the necessary component inequality for every Hamiltonian graph through six vertices and every S.
claims.search_method: Spanning-cycle deletion argument plus exhaustive separator-set enumeration.

claims.claim: For every c, any graph with a vertex of degree at most n/c admits a polynomial-time valid nil output within radius n/c.
claims.evidence: Choose a minimum-degree vertex v and delete its incident edges. The edit count is deg(v)≤n/c. For n≥2 the result has an isolated vertex and is disconnected, hence non-Hamiltonian; the constant-size smaller case is directly decidable. Selecting v and deleting its edges is polynomial-time. Exact enumeration checked every vertex-isolation edit in every graph through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Direct isolation construction, small-order case analysis, and exhaustive exact validation.

claims.claim: A sublinear-component 2-factor routine would settle the full target for every fixed c.
claims.evidence: Let the routine's output on Hamiltonian n-vertex graphs have at most b(n)=o(n) components. For fixed c choose N with b(n)−1≤n/c for n≥N. Orders below N are handled by constant-size exhaustive Hamiltonicity search. For larger inputs, first return nil on disconnected graphs or when no 2-factor exists. On a connected graph with returned factor size q, splice when q−1≤n/c. If q−1>n/c, Hamiltonicity would imply q≤b(n) and hence q−1≤n/c, a contradiction, so returning (G,nil) is correct. This is a valid sufficient conditional, not a proof that the hypothesized routine exists.
claims.search_method: Direct asymptotic quantifier analysis and contraposition; finite checking is inapplicable to the hypothesized o(n) guarantee.

claims.claim: For every c>3, high minimum degree alone cannot guarantee a Hamiltonian graph within n/c edits.
claims.evidence: For every c>3 and n=3q, take G=K_{q,2q}. Then δ(G)=q=n/3>n/c. In any cyclic ordering, if x and z count consecutive pairs lying respectively in the large and small part, degree counting along the ordering gives x−z=q; hence at least x+z≥q cycle edges are absent from G. Every Hamiltonian supergraph therefore needs at least q additions, while arranging the large part into q nonempty blocks separated by small-part vertices attains exactly q additions. Thus the edit distance to every Hamiltonian graph is q>n/c. The exact checker confirmed the minimum for K_{2,4}, used Fraction arithmetic for representative radii, and checked explicit upper-bound cycles for five multiples.
claims.search_method: Exact cyclic part-incidence counting, explicit attaining construction, and rational-arithmetic checks.

claims.claim: The n/3 component bound for an arbitrary 2-factor remains tight even under the promise that the graph is Hamiltonian.
claims.evidence: For n=3q with q≥2, place triangle edges on q disjoint triples. Ordering first one designated vertex from every triple, then the second from every triple, then the third, gives a spanning cyclic order whose consecutive vertices, including the wraparound pair, belong to different triples. Adding those cyclic edges makes the graph Hamiltonian while retaining the q=n/3 triangle components as a 2-factor. Thus a freely chosen 2-factor can attain the bound even though another 2-factor is Hamiltonian. The checker verified this construction for q=2,3,4,5.
claims.search_method: Explicit infinite construction and exact verification of factor degrees, component counts, and spanning cycles.

target_evidence: The exact target requires a polynomial-time sidestep algorithm, or a disproof, for every fixed c>0 on every graph. The draft rigorously gives such an algorithm for 0<c≤3 and gives additional correct promise-class, obstruction, and conditional results for arbitrary c, so it makes material progress. It neither supplies a universal algorithm for c>3 nor disproves one: the complete-bipartite family in claim 8 only defeats a Hamiltonian-completion strategy and is itself immediately eligible for a correct nil output. Accordingly the target is not fully resolved. The final writeup explicitly says the universal c>3 case remains unresolved, and claimed_resolution is PARTIAL, so that resolution label is accurate rather than overstated or understated.
